questions.question: How does the System Design Primer distinguish between a performance problem and a scalability problem?
correctAnswers: A performance problem means the system is slow for a single user; a scalability problem means the system is fast for a single user but slow under heavy load.
wrongAnswers: A performance problem relates to database storage limits, while a scalability problem relates to network cable bandwidth.
A performance problem occurs only on mobile devices, while a scalability problem occurs on desktop servers.
A performance problem means the network is disconnected; a scalability problem means the CPU is overheating.

questions.question: What is the key difference between latency and throughput?
correctAnswers: Latency is the time required to perform an action or produce a result, while throughput is the number of actions or results per unit of time.
wrongAnswers: Latency measures total disk storage capacity, while throughput measures RAM memory usage.
Latency is the number of users logged in simultaneously, while throughput is the ping time to the router.
Latency refers to write operations only, while throughput refers to read operations only.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly describe vertical scaling versus horizontal scaling?
correctAnswers: Vertical scaling (scaling up) adds more resources (CPU, RAM) to a single server.
Horizontal scaling (scaling out) adds more commodity machines to the resource pool.
Horizontal scaling generally results in higher availability and cost efficiency than vertical scaling on enterprise hardware.
wrongAnswers: Vertical scaling requires dividing data across multiple geographic datacenters.
Horizontal scaling simplifies application architecture by eliminating the need for stateless servers.
Vertical scaling is cheaper and easier to auto-scale dynamically than horizontal commodity scaling.

questions.question: What architectural requirement is necessary for web servers when scaling horizontally behind a load balancer?
correctAnswers: Web servers should be stateless, storing user session data in a centralized store or persistent cache.
wrongAnswers: Web servers must store all user session files locally on their local hard drives.
Each web server must maintain a direct hardware cable connection to every other web server.
Web servers must operate without any database connection.

questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, which guarantees are traded off against each other in a distributed system during a network partition?
correctAnswers: Consistency (CP system: every read receives the most recent write or an error)
Availability (AP system: every request receives a response without guarantee of latest version)
wrongAnswers: Throughput vs Storage capacity
Latency vs Bandwidth frequency
Encryption strength vs Compression ratio

questions.question: Which consistency pattern guarantees that after a write, all subsequent reads will immediately see the updated data?
correctAnswers: Strong consistency
wrongAnswers: Weak consistency
Eventual consistency
Soft-state consistency

questions.question: In which scenarios is weak consistency acceptable according to system design guidelines?
correctAnswers: Real-time VoIP calls
Video chat applications
Real-time multiplayer games
wrongAnswers: Financial banking transaction ledgers
E-commerce order payment processing
Relational database ACID transaction logs

questions.question: What is the difference between active-passive and active-active fail-over patterns?
correctAnswers: In active-passive, heartbeats are sent between servers and only the active server handles traffic until failure.
In active-active, both servers actively manage traffic and spread the load between them.
wrongAnswers: Active-passive servers both process writes simultaneously without heartbeats.
Active-active configuration is used exclusively for offline data backups.
Active-passive failover requires no passive standby hardware.

questions.question: How is total system availability calculated when two independent components with availability < 100% are placed in sequence versus in parallel?
correctAnswers: In sequence, overall availability decreases: Total = Availability(A) * Availability(B).
In parallel, overall availability increases: Total = 1 - (1 - Availability(A)) * (1 - Availability(B)).
wrongAnswers: In sequence, availability increases by taking the simple arithmetic sum.
In parallel, availability decreases to the availability of the weakest node squared.
Sequence and parallel arrangements yield identical mathematical availability.

questions.question: What is the acceptable downtime per year for a system advertised as having 99.99% availability ('four 9s')?
correctAnswers: Approximately 52.6 minutes per year
wrongAnswers: Approximately 8.7 hours per year
Approximately 3 days per year
0 seconds per year

questions.question: Which DNS record types correctly match their definitions?
correctAnswers: A record: Points a domain name to an IPv4 address.
CNAME: Points a domain name to another canonical name or A record.
NS record: Specifies the authoritative name servers for a domain.
MX record: Specifies the mail exchange servers for accepting email.
wrongAnswers: TTL record: Encrypts incoming DNS queries.
B-tree record: Stores relational database indexes.
HTTP record: Directs web browsers to execute JavaScript.

questions.question: How do Push CDNs and Pull CDNs differ in content management and site traffic suitability?
correctAnswers: Push CDNs receive content directly uploaded when changes occur on the server; suitable for small traffic or rarely updated sites.
Pull CDNs grab content from the origin server when the first user requests it; suitable for heavy traffic sites with frequently requested content.
wrongAnswers: Pull CDNs store all historical database records permanently, while Push CDNs clear cache every second.
Push CDNs are strictly for mobile devices, while Pull CDNs are for desktop web browsers.
Pull CDNs push content automatically before any user visits the site.

questions.question: What are primary advantages of serving static content (images, JS, CSS, video) from a Content Delivery Network (CDN)?
correctAnswers: Users receive content from edge data centers geographically closer to them, reducing latency.
Origin servers are relieved from fulfilling requests served directly by the CDN.
wrongAnswers: CDNs automatically rewrite SQL database queries for faster execution.
CDNs remove the need for web application code.
CDNs convert all relational databases into NoSQL document stores.

questions.question: What are the primary differences between Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing?
correctAnswers: Layer 4 load balancing inspects transport-layer headers (IP addresses and ports) without reading packet payload contents.
Layer 7 load balancing inspects application-layer data (HTTP headers, cookies, message content) to make routing decisions.
Layer 7 load balancing allows routing based on content type (e.g., directing video requests to video-optimized server clusters).
Layer 4 load balancing consumes fewer CPU and memory resources than Layer 7 load balancing.
wrongAnswers: Layer 4 load balancing operates strictly inside database storage engines.
Layer 7 load balancing cannot perform SSL termination or cookie routing.
Layer 4 load balancing terminates HTTP client connections and reads HTTP cookies.

questions.question: What benefits does SSL Termination provide when configured on a load balancer or reverse proxy?
correctAnswers: It decrypts incoming client requests and encrypts server responses at the proxy level.
It relieves backend application servers from performing computationally expensive SSL/TLS encryption operations.
It eliminates the need to install X.509 certificates on every backend server.
wrongAnswers: It eliminates the need for user passwords across all web applications.
It automatically fixes SQL injection vulnerabilities in application code.
It converts incoming HTTP traffic into UDP datagrams.

questions.question: In what ways does a Reverse Proxy differ from a standard Load Balancer?
correctAnswers: A reverse proxy is useful even with a single web server to provide security, response compression, SSL termination, and static content caching.
A load balancer is primarily deployed across multiple servers serving the same function to distribute incoming traffic.
wrongAnswers: Reverse proxies can only handle database queries, whereas load balancers handle web traffic.
Load balancers hide backend server IP addresses, while reverse proxies expose all backend IP addresses to clients.
Reverse proxies operate exclusively on hardware appliances, while load balancers are software-only.

questions.question: Which of the following routing algorithms can be used by load balancers to distribute traffic?
correctAnswers: Random
Least loaded
Session / Cookie persistence
Round robin or weighted round robin
wrongAnswers: Hard drive serial number hashing
Operating system version matching
Client screen resolution sorting

questions.question: What properties define ACID transactions in relational databases (RDBMS)?
correctAnswers: Atomicity: Each transaction is all or nothing.
Consistency: Any transaction brings the database from one valid state to another.
Isolation: Executing transactions concurrently yields the same result as serial execution.
Durability: Once committed, transaction data remains committed.
wrongAnswers: Availability: Every read request returns a result within 1 ms.
Soft state: The database state changes dynamically without input.
Eventual consistency: Data updates propagate asynchronously after several minutes.

questions.question: What are valid strategies for scaling a Relational Database Management System (RDBMS)?
correctAnswers: Master-slave and master-master replication
Database federation (functional partitioning)
Database sharding (horizontal partitioning)
Denormalization and SQL tuning/indexing
wrongAnswers: Switching all queries from TCP to UDP
Replacing SQL tables with plain text file logs without indexes
Executing all database writes over DNS TXT records

questions.question: What are the trade-offs of Master-Slave database replication?
correctAnswers: Master handles reads and writes; slaves handle read-only traffic.
If master fails, system operates read-only until a slave is promoted to master.
Replication lag can occur if heavy write loads bog down read slaves replaying writes.
wrongAnswers: Slaves process write transactions faster than masters by using multi-threaded writes.
Master-slave replication guarantees zero replication lag under all network conditions.
Slaves automatically handle master election without any additional logic or failover mechanism.

questions.question: What is database federation (functional partitioning)?
correctAnswers: Splitting up databases by function (e.g., separate databases for users, products, and forums).
wrongAnswers: Splitting a single table row across multiple geographical datacenters based on hash values.
Converting relational SQL tables into graph database nodes.
Combining all application databases into a single monolithic schema.

questions.question: What disadvantages or challenges are associated with database sharding?
correctAnswers: Application logic must be updated to route queries to appropriate shards.
Data distribution can become lopsided if power users end up on a single shard.
Joining data across multiple shards is significantly more complex.
Rebalancing shards adds architectural and operational complexity.
wrongAnswers: Sharding prevents the use of database primary keys.
Sharding forces all data to reside exclusively in RAM without disk backup.
Sharding disables parallel write capabilities across the database cluster.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of database denormalization?
correctAnswers: Improving read performance by writing redundant copies of data into tables to avoid expensive database JOINs.
wrongAnswers: Reducing disk space usage by eliminating all duplicate data fields.
Ensuring strict 3rd Normal Form compliance across all tables.
Preventing SQL injection attacks on user login forms.

questions.question: Which of the following schema optimization guidelines are recommended for SQL tuning?
correctAnswers: Use CHAR instead of VARCHAR for fixed-length fields to allow fast random access.
Use DECIMAL for currency fields to avoid floating point representation errors.
Set NOT NULL constraints where applicable to improve search performance.
Avoid storing large BLOBs directly in tables; store location paths/pointers instead.
wrongAnswers: Use VARCHAR for all fixed-length single-character flags.
Use FLOAT or DOUBLE for exact financial currency transactions.
Remove all primary key constraints to speed up full table scans.

questions.question: Which of the following are categorized as NoSQL databases?
correctAnswers: Key-value stores (e.g., Redis, Memcached)
Document stores (e.g., MongoDB, CouchDB)
Wide column stores (e.g., Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra)
Graph databases (e.g., Neo4j, FlockDB)
wrongAnswers: Relational B-tree engines (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL)
Flat CSV spreadsheet files
In-memory CPU registers

questions.question: What properties define the BASE model commonly associated with NoSQL databases?
correctAnswers: Basically Available: The system guarantees availability.
Soft state: System state may change over time without explicit input.
Eventual consistency: System will become consistent over time if given no new input.
wrongAnswers: B-tree Indexed: All records are indexed in balanced trees.
Atomic Transactions: Every multi-document transaction is atomic.
Strict Isolation: Concurrent transactions yield identical serial execution.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid cache update strategies described in the System Design Primer?
correctAnswers: Cache-aside (lazy loading)
Write-through
Write-behind (write-back)
Refresh-ahead
wrongAnswers: Read-around bypass
Cache-invalidation-first
Double-checked locking cache

questions.question: How does the Cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern operate during a read request?
correctAnswers: The application looks for entry in cache; on a cache miss, it reads from DB, writes to cache, and returns entry.
wrongAnswers: The cache automatically intercepts DB queries and updates storage asynchronously before returning.
The DB pushes updates directly to client browsers without application involvement.
The cache clears all existing keys whenever a read miss occurs.

questions.question: What is a main disadvantage of the Write-through caching strategy?
correctAnswers: Overall write operations are slower because data is written synchronously to both cache and underlying data store.
wrongAnswers: Subsequent read operations of newly written data suffer high latency.
Cache entries are always stale and out of sync with the database.
Data in the cache is deleted immediately after being written.

questions.question: What risk is associated with the Write-behind (write-back) caching strategy?
correctAnswers: Risk of data loss if the cache node crashes before queued write entries are persisted to the database.
wrongAnswers: High read latency on every request.
Database locks up on every write operation.
Cache capacity is limited to 10 keys.

questions.question: Which memory eviction algorithm is commonly used in in-memory caches like Redis or Memcached to maintain hot data in memory?
correctAnswers: Least Recently Used (LRU)
wrongAnswers: First In First Out (FIFO) only
Random Key Deletion
Shortest Job First (SJF)

questions.question: At which levels of a web application architecture can caching be implemented?
correctAnswers: Client / Browser side
CDN level
Web server / Reverse proxy level
Database level
Application / In-memory level (e.g. Redis, Memcached)
wrongAnswers: Hardware CPU clock generator level only
Ethernet physical copper cable level only
Power supply unit level only

questions.question: How do message queues enable asynchronous processing in web applications?
correctAnswers: Applications publish job messages to a queue and immediately acknowledge the request to the user.
Background worker processes pick up jobs from the queue, process them asynchronously, and signal task completion.
wrongAnswers: Message queues convert all asynchronous tasks into synchronous HTTP GET calls.
Message queues force clients to block and wait until background jobs finish.
Message queues bypass application servers and write directly to disk drives.

questions.question: What is back pressure and how does it protect message queues under extreme traffic spikes?
correctAnswers: Back pressure limits queue size to prevent queues from exceeding memory capacity.
When queue limits are reached, the system returns HTTP 503 (Server Busy), prompting clients to retry later with exponential backoff.
wrongAnswers: Back pressure automatically deletes all database tables to free up RAM.
Back pressure increases CPU clock speed to process infinite messages in zero time.
Back pressure forces all network packets to travel backwards.

questions.question: What guarantees does Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) provide over User Datagram Protocol (UDP)?
correctAnswers: Connection-oriented connection established via handshake.
Guaranteed delivery of packets in original order without corruption (sequence numbers & checksums).
Automatic packet retransmission upon timeout and flow/congestion control.
wrongAnswers: Zero packet overhead and lower latency than UDP.
Ability to broadcast packets to all devices on a subnet without IP addresses.
Unordered datagram delivery without handshakes.

questions.question: In which scenarios is UDP preferred over TCP?
correctAnswers: Real-time VoIP calls and video streaming where lowest latency is critical.
Real-time multiplayer games where late data is worse than lost data.
Broadcasting messages (e.g. DHCP IP requests).
wrongAnswers: Financial banking transactions requiring exact data integrity.
SSH remote terminal sessions.
Database file sync backups.

questions.question: Which HTTP methods are considered idempotent according to HTTP specifications?
correctAnswers: GET
PUT
DELETE
wrongAnswers: POST
PATCH

questions.question: What are key differences between Remote Procedure Call (RPC) and Representational State Transfer (REST)?
correctAnswers: RPC focuses on exposing behaviors/actions; REST focuses on exposing resources/data.
RPC is often used for high-performance internal microservice communication.
REST enforces a stateless client/server model using uniform HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and URIs.
wrongAnswers: REST requires binary stubs generated by Protobuf compiler, while RPC uses browser HTML.
RPC is restricted strictly to public HTTP APIs, while REST is for internal sockets.
REST requires permanent TCP socket connections, while RPC operates on DNS.

questions.question: What are the four suggested steps for approaching a system design interview question?
correctAnswers: Step 1: Outline use cases, constraints, and assumptions (scope requirements).
Step 2: Create a high-level design (sketch main components and connections).
Step 3: Design core components (dive into details, data schemas, algorithms).
Step 4: Scale the design (identify bottlenecks, trade-offs, caching, sharding).
wrongAnswers: Step 1: Write raw assembly code for the operating system kernel.
Step 2: Install hardware servers physically in a rack.
Step 3: Memorize company financial statements.

questions.question: In back-of-the-envelope estimations, which powers of two approximations are commonly used?
correctAnswers: 2^10 = 1,024 ≈ 1 Thousand (1 KB)
wrongAnswers: 2^10 = 1 Million
2^20 = 1 Billion
2^30 = 1 Trillion

questions.question: According to 'Latency numbers every programmer should know', what are approximate time orders for system operations?
correctAnswers: L1 cache reference: ~0.5 ns
Main memory reference: ~100 ns
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory: ~250 us
Read 1 MB sequentially from SSD: ~1,000 us (1 ms)
Read 1 MB sequentially from HDD: ~30,000 us (30 ms)
wrongAnswers: Main memory reference: 5 seconds
L1 cache reference: 10 milliseconds
SSD sequential read: 30 minutes

questions.question: Which of the following are common Object-Oriented Design (OOD) interview questions included in the System Design Primer?
correctAnswers: Design a hash map
Design a least recently used (LRU) cache
Design a call center
Design a deck of cards
Design a parking lot
Design a chat server
wrongAnswers: Design a x86 CPU microprocessor silicon die
Design a quantum computer operating system
Design a compiler for Rust

questions.question: What design considerations arise when implementing an LRU (Least Recently Used) cache data structure?
correctAnswers: Combining a Doubly Linked List with a Hash Map to achieve O(1) lookups, insertions, and deletions.
wrongAnswers: Using a single unsorted array requiring O(N) linear scans on every lookup.
Storing all cached items in a SQL relational database table on disk.
Using a binary tree requiring O(N log N) sorting on every write.

questions.question: What foundational security practices should be applied to modern web systems?
correctAnswers: Encrypt data both in transit (TLS/SSL) and at rest.
Sanitize user inputs and use parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection and Cross-Site Scripting (XSS).
Enforce the Principle of Least Privilege across service accounts and permissions.
wrongAnswers: Store user passwords in plain text in cache for fast comparison.
Disable all firewall rules on public load balancers.
Expose internal database admin ports directly to the internet.
